[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: English 'while' means 'during the time that', so the activity stops the instant the condition stops holding (the 'while demon'). A Java while tests its condition only before each pass; a pass that has started always finishes.
[1] misconception (M) -> LoopTerminatingCondition: wrong rule: For and while loops end when the condition becomes true. Right rule: A for or while loop ends when its condition becomes false.
[2] misconception (M) -> WhileStopsMidBody: wrong rule: The loop stops the moment the condition becomes false, even in the middle of the body. Right rule: The condition is tested only before each pass, so the whole body finishes before the loop can stop.
[3] misconception (M) -> LoopForOneTimeTest: wrong rule: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once. Right rule: A test made once is an if; a loop repeats.
[4] misconception (M) -> LoopImpliedByOneTest: wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. Right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.
[5] misconception (M) -> ProgramEndsAfterLoop: wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. Right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.
[6] misconception (M) -> LoopCountByIntent: wrong rule: How many times a loop runs is decided by what the program is meant to do, so it may go on after its condition is false. Right rule: The loop runs only while its condition is true when tested; it stops at the first false test.
[7] misconception (M) -> LoopConditionValidatedLater: wrong rule: If a loop condition is false at first but would become true later, the loop still runs (it repeats or skips until the condition is true, then runs until it is false). Right rule: A while loop whose condition is false at the first test runs zero times; nothing later revives it.
[8] misconception (M) -> SingleIterationInsteadOfLoop: wrong rule: A task that must be repeated is written once, without a loop, as if one pass were enough. Right rule: A step that must happen several times (or an unknown number of times) needs a loop such as while or for; code without a loop runs once.
[9] inconsistent_trace (T) -> LoopTerminatingCondition: Applies the while rule (LT) unevenly: tests the condition before some passes but not others, stops in the middle of a body on one pass, or runs the first pass without testing. (here mixing in: "For and while loops end when the condition becomes true")
[10] misconception (M) -> IfIsLoop: wrong rule: an if body repeats while its condition holds. Right rule: An if body runs at most once; only a loop repeats its body.
[11] misconception (M) -> LoopBodyAlwaysOnce: wrong rule: The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start. Right rule: A while or for body runs zero times when the condition is false at the start.
[12] misconception (M) -> InfiniteLoopUnnoticed: wrong rule: a condition that never goes false still terminates. Right rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops.
[13] misconception (M) -> JavaDetectsInfiniteLoops: wrong rule: If my loop never ends, the compiler or Java will warn me. Right rule: Java cannot detect infinite loops in general; you must check that the loop condition eventually becomes false.
[14] misconception (M) -> ForWhileNotInterchangeable: wrong rule: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while. Right rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update.
[15] misconception (M) -> FalseLoopRepeatsNextCode: wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. Right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.
[16] misconception (M) -> LoopVariableNotUpdated: wrong rule: A while loop ends by itself even if nothing in the body changes the variable tested in the condition. Right rule: If no statement in the body changes a variable in the condition, a condition that was true stays true and the loop never ends.

[0] names_the_element (N): The while statement is a loop (iteration statement): it repeats a body as long as a boolean condition is true.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Syntax: while (<boolean expression>) { <statements> } (braces optional for one statement). Meaning: if the expression is false do nothing; if true, execute the body, then check the expression again, and continue as long as it is true.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): 1. Evaluate the condition. 2. If false, skip the body and continue after the loop. 3. If true, execute the whole body, then go back to step 1.
[1] output_prediction (OP): A while statement has no value; its result is the state and output after the passes it made: e.g. TenHellos with i = 4 and i <= 10 prints 4th to 10th Hello (7 passes) and leaves i = 11.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One pass: test the condition with the current values, then (if true) apply every body statement once in order; the variables assigned in the body change and nothing else; a false test ends the loop with the state unchanged.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The loop condition is a boolean expression evaluated before every pass; the loop stops the first time it is false, so the body must eventually make it false.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): do { body } while (c); means the same as while (c) { body } except that the first test is omitted, so the body runs at least once.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): break exits the loop immediately, so a while loop can end either by a false test or by a break; while (true) needs a break (or is infinite).
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): An animation repeats clear/draw/show/pause steps inside a loop, typically one that runs indefinitely.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): A convergence test is the while condition that keeps refining an estimate until the error is within tolerance, e.g. while (Math.abs(t - c/t) > epsilon * t).
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): The body is the block that the while repeats; it runs only after a true test and is completed before the next test.
[6] relation_to_neighbour (R): The while condition usually tests a loop variable that is initialized before the loop and updated in the body; if the body never changes it, the loop never ends.
[7] relation_to_neighbour (R): To trust a while loop, state what stays true on every pass and why the condition eventually becomes false (e.g. v is always a power of 2, v increases, so the loop terminates).
[8] relation_to_neighbour (R): Binary conversion uses while loops: one to find the largest power of 2 <= N, and one to cast out powers of 2 in decreasing order.
[9] relation_to_neighbour (R): if and while have the same form, but if tests its condition once and runs the block at most once, while while tests again after every pass and repeats the block as long as the condition is true.
[10] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: indefinite (event-controlled) repetition - repeat until something happens whose number of passes is not known in advance (until convergence, until broke or goal); the condition variable is often a stepper or most-recent holder.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> LoopTerminatingCondition: Changing < to <= adds exactly one pass at the boundary; removing the update from the body makes a loop that was entered never end; a condition that is false initially gives zero passes whatever the body does. Rewriting as for (init; cond; update) preserves behaviour if no continue is involved.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A while loop tests its condition before the first pass, using the values set before the loop. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Initializations before the loop that already make the condition false (e.g. boolean done = true; while (!done) ...): the body runs zero times and no error is reported.
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use while when the number of passes depends on what happens during the loop (convergence, input, simulation) or the loop variable is needed after the loop; use for for counted loops, do-while when the body must run at least once, and if when the test is needed only once.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A ; right after if (...) is an empty statement that forms the whole then branch; the following statement or block is no longer part of the if. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Any if (cond); followed by a statement or block: that statement runs for every input, whatever cond is (it compiles without error).
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A ; right after while (...) or for (...) is an empty statement that is the whole loop body; the block written next is not repeated. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: for (...); { body } runs the body once after the loop ends; while (cond); with a cond that the empty body cannot change hangs forever (infinite loop) when cond starts true.
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The body must eventually make the condition false. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: No body statement changes a variable in the condition, or the update moves away from the bound (e.g. while (i > 3) i = i + 1;): infinite loop, endless output or a hang; Java cannot detect it in general.

if and while have the same form, but if tests its condition once and runs the block at most once, while while tests again after every pass and repeats the block as long as the condition is true.
A while tests its boolean condition before every pass and stops the first time it evaluates to false.
BouncingBall repeats erase, draw at the new position, and show with a pause inside a while (true) loop.
break immediately exits a loop without letting it run to completion.
continue ends the current pass of the while loop and goes straight back to the loop test.
The convergence test is the condition of a while loop that keeps refining an estimate until the error is below a tolerance.
do { body } while (c); is a while loop whose test is moved to the bottom.
A while loop whose condition never becomes false never ends.
The loop body is the block of statements that a while (or for) loop repeats on each pass.

A while loop has the same three control parts as a for loop, written in other places: the index set before the loop, the loop-continuation condition in the header, and the update as the last statement of the body.
To reason about a while loop you state what stays true on every pass and why the condition eventually becomes false.
A loop variable is a counter that the loop initializes, tests in its condition and increments on each pass.
Binary conversion repeats one step in a while loop: find the largest power of 2 not above n, output a bit and subtract.
A sentinel loop is a while loop whose condition tests each value read against the stop value.
